+Accepts an `email` and `password`. On success, it will return the logged in user as well as a token that can be used to authenticate. With [refresh tokens](./overview#refresh-tokens), it also returns a `refreshToken`. In the GraphQL and REST APIs, this operation also automatically sets an HTTP-only cookie including the user's token. If you pass a `res` to the Local API operation, Payload will set a cookie there as well.

Allows for "refreshing" JWTs. If your user has a token that is about to expire, but the user is still active and using the app, you might want to use the `refresh` operation to receive a new token by executing this operation via the authenticated user.
-This operation requires a non-expired token to send back a new one. If the user's token has already expired, you will need to allow them to log in again to retrieve a new token.

+This operation requires a non-expired token to send back a new one. If the user's token has already expired, you will need to allow them to log in again to retrieve a new token, unless you use [refresh tokens](./overview#refresh-tokens). Then send `{ refreshToken }` in the request body, or as the `refreshToken` argument in GraphQL, and the response also includes the next `refreshToken`.
If successful, this operation will automatically renew the user's HTTP-only cookie and will send back the updated token in JSON.

| **`lockTime`**                 | Set the time (in milliseconds) that a user should be locked out if they fail authentication more times than `maxLoginAttempts` allows for.                                                                                  |

| **`loginWithUsername`**        | Ability to allow users to login with username/password. [More](/docs/authentication/overview#login-with-username)                                                                                                           |

| **`maxLoginAttempts`**         | Only allow a user to attempt logging in X amount of times. Automatically locks out a user from authenticating if this limit is passed. Set to `0` to disable.                                                               |

+| **`refreshTokens`**            | Set to `true` to also return a refresh token from login, which keeps clients logged in after their token expires. [More details](#refresh-tokens).                                                                          |

| **`removeTokenFromResponses`** | Set to true if you want to remove the token from the returned authentication API responses such as login or refresh.                                                                                                        |

| **`strategies`**               | Advanced - an array of custom authentication strategies to extend this collection's authentication with. [More details](./custom-strategies).                                                                               |

| **`tokenExpiration`**          | How long (in seconds) to keep the user logged in. JWTs and HTTP-only cookies will both expire at the same time.                                                                                                             |

+Apps that aren't always running, like mobile apps or CLIs, can't refresh their token before it expires. With `refreshTokens`, login also returns a refresh token, which the [refresh operation](./operations#refresh) trades for a new token and a new refresh token, even after the token expired:
+      // Optional. How many seconds the session lasts without a refresh, which is how long its
+      // refresh token can be used. Defaults to 30 days.
+// Store the new refresh token for next time

+Refresh tokens don't expire on their own. They work as long as their session, which lasts `expiration` from the last refresh instead of `tokenExpiration`. The token itself still expires after `tokenExpiration`.

+Each refresh token is meant to be used once, so store the new one after every refresh. For 30 seconds after a refresh, the refresh token from right before it still works, so clients that refresh twice at once stay logged in. If a used refresh token comes back otherwise, Payload treats it as copied and logs out its session. Logging out ends refresh tokens too. They require `useSessions`, and aren't returned with `removeTokenFromResponses`.

All auth-related operations are available via Payload's REST, Local, and GraphQL APIs. These operations are automatically added to your Collection when you enable Authentication. [More details](./operations).

+Auth collections with `useSessions` (the default) now store two more fields on each session, `refreshCount` and `refreshedAt`. [Refresh tokens](../authentication/overview#refresh-tokens) use them to tell the latest refresh token apart from older ones.

+On SQL adapters this adds two columns to each `<collection>_sessions` table, so existing projects need a database migration. In development the schema is pushed automatically; in production, generate a migration with `payload migrate:create` and run `payload migrate`. Existing sessions keep working, since an empty `refreshCount` counts as `0`. MongoDB needs no migration.
### Local API access is now enforced by default #overrideaccess-now-defaults-to-false-on-local-api-operations

`overrideAccess` now defaults to `false` on Local API operations, so omitting it respects Access Control instead. Operations that do not expose `overrideAccess`, and operations such as `resetPassword` where it was already required or did not default to `true`, are unaffected by this change.
